source.title: Training LLMs over Neurally Compressed Text
source.authors: Brian Lester; Jaehoon Lee; Alexander A. Alemi; Jeffrey Pennington; Adam Roberts; Jascha Narain Sohl-Dickstein; Noah Constant

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures held-out language-model loss across model sizes in a new text-training setting: models trained on neurally compressed text. It does not reproduce the original scaling-law fits.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out bits/byte across four M2 sizes for several tokenization and compression settings. These results bear on loss as model size changes, but the paper does not fit a power law or test small-run extrapolation, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or architecture-shape effects. It also reports compression/decompression and spelling experiments; those do not test the listed scaling-law versions. The cited scaling-law results themselves are not extracted as findings.
record.test_reason: The study trains M2 models at four sizes (25m–2b non-embedding parameters, about two orders of magnitude) on a fixed 26.2B tokens. It reports held-out C4 bits/byte for ten tokenization or compression settings, so its results bear on whether loss falls with parameter count in a new text-pretraining setting (compressed-text tokens). It fits no power law. Scale is used mainly as a lens for comparing tokenizers.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that naive Arithmetic Coding compressed text is unlearnable and that Equal-Info Windows make it learnable. Their best EqualInfoAC models beat byte-level baselines at matched inference FLOPs/byte and approach SentencePiece as scale rises to 2b, while using shorter sequences. They add that GZip is learnable but uncompetitive, and that core trends persist when training data is scaled with model size.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains models over multiple text tokenizations and reports held-out bits/byte across model sizes; it does not fit Kaplan-style scaling laws or estimate compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary substantially with compression/tokenization method, Equal-Info window length, and M2 vocabulary size. The paper also reports that scaling training data proportionally with model size changes absolute slopes but leaves the core method trends unchanged.
record.problems: The main parameter range is 25m to 2b, and the authors state that the 2b models remain undertrained at 200,000 steps. Most scaling-sweep values are reported without uncertainty; five-seed variability is reported for 25m models, with the largest standard deviation 0.0061 bits/byte. No power-law fit or extrapolation test is provided.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix D.3 reports a separate proportional-training-data checkpoint sweep (Table 13) and says core trends are unchanged; its individual model/checkpoint values are omitted to keep the record focused on the main fixed-token sweep. The two raw-bitstream models in Section 5.1 and sequence-to-sequence compression/decompression experiments in Section 5.2 are not parameter-size scaling sweeps.

untested.parts: No power-law fit or functional-form check; only four sizes. Tokens and compute are not varied independently. Data is fixed at 26.2B tokens, so the 2b models are undertrained, as the authors note, and data may be a bottleneck.
No compute-optimal allocation sweep. Appendix D.3 only re-reads checkpoints at a Chinchilla-style data-to-parameter ratio.
Depth and width are not varied at fixed parameter count.
Text only; no other modalities, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling.
No downstream scaling. The spelling fine-tune uses a single 403m size.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: Size sweeps for EqualInfoAC with b=32, 64 and 128 windows (v=256 and v=65k). b=32 improves clearly (2.05→1.65 for v=256); b=64 and b=128 are nearly flat, e.g. b=128 v=256 stays at 1.71 at all sizes. This is relevant to the flat-scaling scope limit.
missing.locator: Section 4 'Short Windows are the Best', Fig. 5, Appendix D.9 Table 16

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its V1 evidence is weak: four sizes, no fit, fixed data. The Chinchilla-proportional checkpoint sweep (Appendix D.3, Table 13) is declared in rows_left_out but is arguably the cleaner V1 test, since it removes the data bottleneck; it shows steeper but still monotone declines for learnable settings and flat uniform loss for AC and StaticAC. The AC and StaticAC flatness reflects failure to learn, not a bent power law.

versions.untested_parts: The paper measures loss as parameter count varies, but does not fit or establish a power-law form, test several orders of magnitude, or independently vary tokens and compute while holding the other quantities non-bottlenecking.
No laws fit on small runs are used to predict larger runs.
No compute-budget sweep identifies loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations.
The paper does not vary depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The study uses English text pretraining; it does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream task performance is measured.
The study does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, nor test whether fitted curves bend away from power laws.

relationships.condition: Learnable tokenizations (Bytes, SentencePiece, EqualInfoAC[b=16] v=256 and v=65k, GZip v=256 and v=65k), 25m–2b, fixed 26.2B tokens
relationships.reason: Bits/byte falls monotonically at every size step, with diminishing gains, e.g. Bytes 1.29→1.03 and SentencePiece 1.12→0.87 (R01–R08, R25–R40). The power-law form itself is not fitted.
relationships.display_finding: Bits per byte decreased at every size step, from 1.29 to 1.03 for Bytes and 1.12 to 0.87 for SentencePiece, without testing a power-law form.

relationships.condition: Arithmetic Coding and StaticAC compressed-text tokens (v=256 and v=65k), 25m–2b
